title: Data Wrangling
text:
NYC Flights: Worst Arrival Delays

library(nycflights13)

worst10_arr_delays <- flights %>%
  filter(!is.na(arr_delay)) %>%
  group_by(day) %>%
  slice_max(arr_delay, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avg_delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(worst10_arr_delays, aes(x = factor(month), y = avg_delay)) +
  geom_col(fill = "cyan") +
  labs(
    title = "Average of Top 10 Worst Arrival Delays per Day by Month",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Average Arrival Delay (Minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








The worst arrival delays happen in the beginning of the year, with the worst occurring in February. This suggests the company can allocate more budget to the first two quarters.

title: Data Wrangling
text:
Temperature Analysis by Month

air.tib %>%
  count(Month, wt = Temp) %>%
  mutate(
    Month = recode(Month,
                   `5` = "May",
                   `6` = "June",
                   `7` = "July",
                   `8` = "August",
                   `9` = "September"),
    Month = factor(Month)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = reorder(Month, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "cyan") +
  labs(
    title = "Total Monthly Temperature",
    x = "Total Temperature",
    y = "Month"

  theme_classic()

title: Data Wrangling
text:
Ozone & Weather Variable Relationships

air.tib %>%
  mutate(temp_wind = Temp / Wind) %>%
  select(Ozone, Temp, Wind, temp_wind) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Temp, Wind, temp_wind),
               names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Relationships Between Ozone and Weather Variables",
    x = "Variable Value",
    y = "Ozone Level"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 111 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









There is a stronger relationship between ozone level and temperature, and ozone level and wind, than between ozone level and temp_wind. There is also a negative relationship between wind and ozone level.

title: Advanced Visualization
text:
Animated Visualization with gganimate
The gganimate package adds animation to charts, giving viewers the ability to observe how patterns change over time or category. This animated chart tracks life expectancy vs. GDP per capita across continents.

library(scales)
library(gapminder)
library(tidyverse)
library(gganimate)
library(gifski)

p_country <- gapminder %>%
  filter(continent != "Oceania") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = dollar, limits = c(200, 10000)) +
  scale_size(range = c(1, 20)) +
  theme_bw() +
  facet_wrap(~continent) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

anim <- p_country +
  labs(x = "GDP Per Capita in USD",
       y = "Life Expectancy in Years",
       title = "Year: {frame_time}",
       subtitle = "Animating Life Expectancy vs. GDP Per Capita over time") +
  transition_time(year) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(
    size = 23,
    face = "bold"
  ))
anim

title: Advanced Visualization
text:
Key Concepts: Scales and Transformations
Scales regulate the association of data values with visual representations of position, size, and color. Key takeaways:

Nonlinear transformations like logarithmic scaling balance skewed data distributions
Custom color palettes enhance accessibility and focus on valuable insights
Theme customization provides consistent visual identity across plots
Minimizing clutter by streamlining extraneous gridlines and decorative features improves readability

title: Advanced Visualization
text:
Useful Visualization Functions
Three functions from David Robinson’s impromptu visualization demonstration:


geom_count()
Visualizes overlapping observations by adjusting point size based on frequency, making dense data easier to interpret.
ggplot2


gganimate()
Enables dynamic visualizations that show change across time or categories, helping viewers understand trends through motion.
Animation


ggplotly()
Allows integration of interactive charts where users can hover over data points and explore detailed values.
Plotly


gt + gtExtra
Converts regular tables into attractive and publication-ready summary reports with mini-visualizations like sparklines and distribution plots.

title: Advanced Visualization
text:
Design Principles from Cédric Scherer
Key tips for improving data visualization:

Color palettes — Use considered palettes that make a difference but are not overwhelming. Adequate choice of colors enhances accessibility and focus on valuable insights.
Theme customization — Personalize themes and types to provide consistent visual identity and enhance professionalism and readability.
Reduce clutter — Minimize extraneous gridlines, labels, and decorative features that divert attention from the data narrative.

title: Coursework Projects
section: Project Title 1: Research Participation & Data Insight Analysis (RPE Project)
text:
Project Title 1: Research Participation & Data Insight Analysis (RPE Project)
This project involved a comprehensive exploratory data analysis of student research participation data to understand how academic background influences perceived value of research engagement.
The analysis focused on transforming raw survey responses into meaningful analytical structures through data cleaning, recoding, and index construction. A key aspect of the project was the development of a composite perception index using multiple survey items, validated using internal consistency measures.
The study further explored differences across academic major groups by aggregating responses and identifying patterns in perceived value. This allowed for a structured comparison of how students from different academic disciplines evaluate the usefulness of participating in research activities.
Beyond descriptive analysis, this project emphasized data preparation workflows, feature engineering, and group-level statistical interpretation, demonstrating how raw survey data can be transformed into actionable insights.

title: Coursework Projects
text:
Project Title 2: Multi-Dataset Analysis & Visualization
This project demonstrates applied data manipulation and visualization across multiple structured datasets, focusing on income, religion, air quality, and transportation data.
The primary objective was to explore how data structure impacts analysis and visualization outcomes. A key focus was reshaping datasets between wide and long formats to enable meaningful comparisons and graphical representation.
The project also involved handling missing values, deriving summary statistics, and constructing visual outputs that reveal relationships between variables such as income distribution patterns, flight delays, and environmental measurements.
A significant analytical component was the transformation of raw tabular datasets into formats suitable for heatmaps, scatter plots, and grouped summaries, highlighting the importance of data preparation in any analytical workflow.

title: Coursework Projects
section: Project Title 3: Advanced Data Visualization & Storytelling
text:
Project Title 3: Advanced Data Visualization & Storytelling
This project focuses on advanced data visualization techniques used to enhance analytical storytelling, interactivity, and temporal interpretation of data.
The analysis integrates dynamic visualization approaches such as animated charts and interactive plots to demonstrate how data relationships evolve over time. These methods allow for deeper exploration of trends that are not easily observable in static visualizations.
In addition, the project explores multi-layer visualization design, including the combination of multiple variables in a single analytical framework. This approach improves the interpretability of complex datasets by reducing cognitive overload while maintaining analytical depth.
A key strength of this project is the emphasis on data storytelling, where visual design choices are intentionally used to communicate insights clearly and effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences.

title: Coursework Projects
section: Project Title 4: Academic Performance & Attendance Analysis
text:
Project Title 4: Academic Performance & Attendance Analysis
This project analyzes student academic performance using structured institutional data, focusing on the relationship between prior academic achievement, attendance behavior, and final academic outcomes.
The analysis explores how prior GPA, ACT scores, and attendance rates jointly influence term performance. Special attention is given to group-based differences, particularly between freshman and non-freshman students, to assess whether academic experience moderates performance outcomes.
The project applies regression analysis, correlation matrices, and distributional comparisons to uncover both linear relationships and group-level behavioral differences. These methods allow for a deeper understanding of how academic behaviors interact with performance outcomes.
A key insight from this project is that academic performance is not solely determined by prior ability, but is also influenced by engagement factors such as attendance and institutional experience level.

text: This section documents data visualization coursework using R, ggplot2, and the Wooldridge attendance dataset. Topics include scatter plots, bar charts, boxplots, correlation heatmaps, and interactive Plotly charts.

title: Data Visualization
section: Scatter Plot: Prior GPA vs Missed Classes
text:
Scatter Plot: Prior GPA vs Missed Classes

df %>%
  mutate(soph = recode(soph, `1` = "Sophomore", `0` = "Non-Sophomore"),
         soph = factor(soph)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(priGPA, missed)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ soph) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Prior GPA and Missed Classes",
    x = "Prior GPA",
    y = "Missed Classes"
  )








There is a negative linear association between Prior GPA and missed classes. This association is present in both groups — sophomore and non-sophomore.

text:
Bar Charts: Final Score by ACT and Sophomore Status

df %>%
  mutate(soph_label = factor(soph, levels = c(0, 1),
                              labels = c("Not Sophomore", "Sophomore"))) %>%
  group_by(ACT, soph_label) %>%
  summarise(mean_final = mean(final, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ACT, y = mean_final, fill = soph_label)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), width = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Not Sophomore" = "orange", "Sophomore" = "lightblue")) +
  labs(title = "Mean Final Score by ACT and Sophomore Status",
       x = "ACT Score", y = "Mean Final Score",
       fill = "Sophomore Status") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Data Visualization
section: Boxplot: Final Scores by ACT and Sophomore Status
text:
Boxplot: Final Scores by ACT and Sophomore Status

df %>%
  mutate(soph_label = factor(soph, levels = c(0, 1),
                              labels = c("Not Sophomore", "Sophomore"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(ACT), y = final, fill = soph_label)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.2, dodge.width = 0.8),
              aes(color = soph_label), alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Not Sophomore" = "yellow", "Sophomore" = "lightblue")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Not Sophomore" = "orange", "Sophomore" = "pink")) +
  labs(title = "Final Scores by ACT and Sophomore Status",
       x = "ACT Score", y = "Final Score",
       fill = "Sophomore Status", color = "Sophomore Status") +
  theme_bw()








The boxplot with jitter delivers a more complete and nuanced summary of the data, showing the distribution’s spread, median, and potential outliers.

section: Working with Vectors and Data Frames
text:
Working with Vectors and Data Frames

library(tidyverse)

# Create vectors
stock_prices <- c(42.5, 43.0, 44.1, 2.7)
stock_company <- c("Microsoft", "Apple", "Facebook", "Tesla")
stock_ticker <- c("MSFT", "AAPL", "FB", "TSLA")
make_cars <- c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)

# Update and name
stock_prices <- stock_prices + 5
names(stock_prices) <- stock_company

# Build data frame
stock_info.df <- data.frame(
  stock_prices,
  stock_company,
  stock_ticker,
  make_cars,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Correct Tesla
stock_info.df[stock_info.df$stock_company == "Tesla", "stock_prices"] <- 47.7

# Add new row
extra <- data.frame(
  stock_prices = 50.4,
  stock_company = "General Motors",
  stock_ticker = "GM",
  make_cars = TRUE
)
stock_info.df <- rbind(stock_info.df, extra)
stock_info.df$open_price <- c(47.3, 47.8, 49.5, 47.9, 55.3)

# Percentage change
stock_info.df$change_percent <-
  ((stock_info.df$stock_prices - stock_info.df$open_price) /
     stock_info.df$open_price) * 100

Functional Programming with purrr
The purrr package simplifies iteration by replacing traditional loops with cleaner functions like map(). Instead of calculating the mean of each column separately, map_dbl() computes all means in a single step.

library(purrr)

cols <- c("mpg", "hp", "wt")
map_dbl(mtcars[cols], mean)

 20.09062 146.68750   3.21725

library(gapminder)
library(forcats)

# Population by continent in 2007
pop_2007 <- gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  summarise(total_pop = sum(pop), .by = continent)

pop_2007 |>
  arrange(desc(total_pop))

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  continent  total_pop
  <fct>          <dbl>
1 Asia      3811953827
2 Africa     929539692
3 Americas   898871184
4 Europe     586098529
5 Oceania     24549947

# Reorder factor levels
gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  summarise(total_pop = sum(pop), .by = continent) |>
  ggplot(aes(fct_reorder(continent, total_pop), total_pop)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Population by Continent (2007)",
       x = "Continent",

text:
Top & Bottom Countries: Life Expectancy

library(patchwork)

asia_2007 <- gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007, continent == "Asia")

# Top 5
top_plot <- asia_2007 |>
  slice_max(lifeExp, n = 5) |>
  ggplot(aes(fct_reorder(country, lifeExp), lifeExp)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 5 Countries")

# Bottom 5
bottom_plot <- asia_2007 |>
  slice_min(lifeExp, n = 5) |>
  ggplot(aes(fct_reorder(country, lifeExp), lifeExp)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Bottom 5 Countries")

top_plot + bottom_plot

title: R Programming
text:
Key Programming Concepts


Custom Functions
Define reusable functions to reduce repetition and make code more readable. Whenever code is repeated more than twice, convert it into a function.
DRY Principle


Functional Iteration
Use map(), map_dbl(), and map_dfr() from purrr instead of traditional for loops for cleaner, more expressive code.
purrr


Factor Reordering
Use fct_reorder() from forcats to arrange categorical variables by a numeric summary for more meaningful visualizations.
forcats


Anonymous Functions
Define functions inline without naming them. This makes code more concise for one-time operations inside pipes.
Functional
